activities.anchor: The mismatch matters because particles differ hugely in weight
activities.caption: call the molecule's weight
activities.name: moleSugarEstimate

config.prompt: A water molecule weighs 18 atomic mass units. Roughly how many does a sugar molecule weigh?
config.why: About 342 — nineteen times heavier, so equal grams of water and sugar never contain equal numbers of molecules.
config.context: Equal grams hide unequal counts — which is exactly why chemists count in moles instead.

activities.caption: pair each formula with what it names
activities.name: moleFormulaMatch

config.prompt: Formula flavours — pair each with what it actually names:

pairs.right: the whole molecule — 6 C, 12 H, 6 O
the 1:1 ratio of ions in the crystal — no molecules at all

config.why: The little numbers are subscripts, and moving one changes the substance: H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, not 'double water'.

activities.anchor: Three working formulas generate all of stoichiometry
activities.caption: file each calculation under its formula
activities.name: moleFormulaBuckets

config.prompt: Three formulas run all of stoichiometry. File each calculation:

items.label: one mole of any gas fills about 24,000 cm³ at 20 °C, 1 atm
12 dm³ of any gas is about 0.5 mol

config.why: Equal volumes of gas hold equal numbers of particles (Avogadro's own hypothesis) — whatever they are made of.

activities.caption: true or false — count or weight
activities.name: moleCountJudge

statements.s: A mole is a count — like a dozen, but for particles — not a weight.
statements.why: Molar mass in g/mol is the bridge that lets the count be found from a weighing, not the definition.

statements.s: One mole of hydrogen gas and one mole of oxygen gas contain the same number of molecules.
Molar mass in g/mol is the definition of the mole.
statements.why: The definition is the count; the molar mass is what makes it weighable.

statements.s: One mole of hydrogen gas (2.016 g) and one mole of oxygen gas (31.998 g) are wildly different weights.
statements.why: The whole point: equal counts, unequal masses.

activities.anchor: It treats a balanced equation as a recipe with two interchangeable readings
activities.caption: run the mole chain, in order
activities.name: moleChainOrder

config.prompt: Every stoichiometry calculation is one chain — put it in order:
items: Measure what you start with — a mass, a volume or a concentration × volume
Convert what you measured to moles
Follow the recipe ratio from the balanced equation
Convert back to the grams (or volume) of the product — watching for the reactant that runs out first
config.why: The ratios of the big numbers are fixed forever, whatever amounts you start with — mole counting is molecule counting scaled up.

activities.anchor: how much water is made by burning 8 g of hydrogen
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the worked recipe
activities.name: moleWaterCloze

config.text: Burning 8 g of hydrogen in unlimited oxygen: moles of H₂ = 8 ÷ 2.016 ≈ %%0%% mol; the recipe's hydrogen-to-water ratio is %%1%%, so water produced = 3.97 × 18.02 ≈ 71.5 g — the other 63.5 g came from the %%2%%.
config.hint: Divide by the molar mass first; the conservation audit names the donor of the extra mass.

activities.caption: one line of the limiting-reagent summary is wrong
activities.name: moleLimitSpot

config.prompt: One line of this limiting-reagent summary is wrong. Find it.
lines: Mix 10 mol of H₂ with 10 mol of O₂ — the recipe wants 2 : 1
10 mol of H₂ needs only 5 mol of O₂ — hydrogen is the limiting reagent
Oxygen is in excess, with 5 mol left over
The limiting reagent is whichever reactant you have fewer moles of
Divide each reactant's moles by its coefficient; the smallest quotient is the limiter
config.correction: The limit is set by the recipe ratio, not the raw counts — 3 mol of hydrogen limits even when oxygen has fewer moles, because it consumes only 1.5 mol of oxygen.
config.why: Reactants are almost never mixed in exact recipe proportions — finding which one runs out first is the first move of every real calculation.

config.prompt: Iron ore is Fe₂O₃ (Mr = 159.7, iron at 55.8). Roughly what percentage of the ore's mass is actually iron?
config.why: About 69.9 per cent — iron contributes 2 × 55.8 = 111.7 of the 159.7. That arithmetic turns a mine's assay report into a business case.
config.context: Percentage composition: the loop closed between formula and mass.
